  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.

  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`

  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.

  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.

  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.

  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.

  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.

  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the

  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle

  the size changes its look (its wave table is in window pixels), so it stays
  at 10.2 fps.

  against a read-everything-first reference in every overlap direction.

  forgets (32 blocks a stop; `leaks` named `fringe_add_intersection`).

  and the picture stays dim. Its pixels go straight to the window as it plots
  them, and the frame's `XPutImage` into a pixmap and copy back are skipped:

  `tools/binaryring_patch.py` makes `frand1`'s exponent literal a float.

  30 fps, so at 10 fps a picture takes about 36 s instead of 12.

  (`tools/etruscanvenus_patch.py`, upstream's 192 by 128) at half resolution;

  `curlicue.h` is copied from `vendor/` at build time (`vendor_data.py`).

  its source, notices row, `blocktube_single_gl.c`, `gl_textures.py` and
  `blocktube_patch.py` stay, the wrapper out of the build filter. To bring
  it back, add `pre:gl_textures.py` to the three `extra_scripts` and
  `blocktube` (with its `count_the_blocks`) to `patch_float_literals.py`
  again. It drew 400 blocks
  (`tools/blocktube_patch.py`, upstream's 1,000) at half resolution with a
  10 ms delay (`"*delay: 10000"` in its registry entry, now gone);
  fog is applied per block from the modelview's z when the hack
  sets the block's colour, and a block the fog hides is not drawn. There is
  no sphere map, so each face shows the whole texture. Its texture is
  converted from `vendor/` at build time (`gl_textures.py`). It also filters

  frame.

  `failed_ports.txt`). Each Companion Cube face draws a 9,588-vertex disc:
  about 71,000 vertices a cube, three cubes by default. Floppy's model is
  26,340 vertices (about 630 KB of floats, which would not fit beside the
  current firmware in the 3 MB app partition).
- Rocks and DecayScreen were wired, looked at and dropped in the 2026-10-12
  second batch, then brought back after Rod asked for the shim to be extended.
  Rocks stamps every rock bigger than 3 pixels with `XCopyPlane` from a
  depth-1 pixmap it filled with `XFillPolygon`, and the shim drew nothing into
  a bitmap, so only the far dots showed (a 3,000-frame dump looked nearly
  black): `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` now fill bitmaps. On the board it

  all but 32 KB of the internal heap while it runs (about 180 of its 400
  bitmaps are under the 4 KB internal limit); a rotation soak that left it for
  DecayScreen read heap and PSRAM back at their idle values. DecayScreen smears
  the picture `load_image_async_simple` paints (see `x11shim.md`); without one
  it stays black. Both were host-only findings from a frame dump: look at later
  frames (3,000) as well as 400 before pinning, and read what the hack draws
  with.
- Penrose (`penrose_short_pause.c`, `tools/penrose_patch.py`) restarts after
  900 frames (about 10 s at 87 fps) instead of 3,141 once the screen is full
  and 31,415 after an error it thinks it can recover from, about six minutes
  at the board's rate with nothing moving. Upstream counts those pauses in
  frames, tuned for a fast X server, so other devices show the same stall.
- Triangle's palette is `make_smooth_colormap`, which the shim now builds the
  way upstream picks it (two to five random colours, any saturation, never
  black): its first version was always a bright rainbow, and every hack that
  asks for a smooth map changed colour with the fix (24 pinned hashes moved,
  all looked at).
- Abstractile holds about 6.1 MB of PSRAM while it runs (the free PSRAM read
  883 KB), so it leaves little for anything else: it stops and restarts clean
  in the leak test, but watch it in a rotation soak. Lisa takes 87 ms a step
  as copied (9.6 fps) and 52 ms in single precision (`lisa_single.c`, 14.3
  fps) with frames that look the same but hash differently. Worm's worms are
  one pixel wide and there are only a few on a 466 pixel screen: plain, for
  Rod to judge. XRaySwarm's host frames are white bugs and trails; whether
  that is its default look or a colour-table gap in the shim is unchecked.

# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).

  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.

  modification history.

  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`

  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a

  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).

  channels with one multiply), and took Starfish from 8.5 to 19 fps. Goop draws

  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is still double

  canvas lacks.

  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and

  pixel-identical by construction;

  152 pixels a burst filled the picture and the glow blur (energy kept, output
  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`

  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.

  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.
- CWaves (`cwaves_single.c`) fills 233 columns, each a 2 by 466 rectangle, so
  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.
- A single-precision wrapper must watch for a hack that passes the address of
  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.
- Moire and Cynosure are paced by their own delays (Moire draws a 20-row chunk
  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.
- Moire2 (`moire2_direct.c`, `moire2_planes.h`, built on Halo's planes) keeps
  its four depth-1 pixmaps as bit planes and adds an outline circle, an XOR
  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.
- Boing was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and plain on a small screen);
  its source, notices row and `boing_gl.c` stay, the wrapper out of the build
  filter. Its 208 scanlines are blended full-width lines and cost half its
  step: 5.0 fps with them, 8.3 without; the ball size barely matters (0.3
  saves 13 ms). HexTrail (`hextrail_single_gl.c`) draws
  every hexagon it has built, so its step climbs from about 19 ms to a ceiling
  and it restarts: use a mean over a cycle (150 s). The grid is `count * 2`
  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:
  mean 5.7 fps at upstream's 20, 9.1 at 10, 12.7 at 6 (registered,
  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled
  (under 10 fps). Single precision gave 13.0; skipping the depth clear it
  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision
  wrapper adapts `get_position` and `get_rotation`: the hack passes `double`
  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).
- Celtic (`celtic_single.c`, issue #37) is registered after HexTrail and takes
  a median step of 32 ms against 832 as copied (`assessment_measured.md.in`).
  The wrapper is single precision (`rint` and `floor` mapped to float: the
  header maps only some libm calls) and frees the colour table that
  `celtic_init` callocs. `tools/celtic_patch.py` does three things at build
  time. It works `t*n - floor(t*n)` out once and clamps it: in float a fused
  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted
  (the 3000-frame test found it). It sizes the graph to the screen: upstream's
  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1
  MB on the host, and 44 of 300 random starts needed more than the board's free
  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it
  scales the 0.0001 animation tick by `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE` (default 4,
  `-DCELTIC_STEP_SCALE=<n>`), which cuts the shadow look-ahead's work and a
  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes
  over 150 starts. Do not shorten `*delay2`: it is a 5 s dwell on the finished
  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
  comes out too small to fill the screen.
- A full-frame write to the PSRAM canvas costs about 25 ms whatever does it
  (memcpy, a 2 by 2 blow-up, 32-bit stores). Eruption at half size
  (`eruption_direct.c`, `lowrez_put.h`, `-DERUPTION_SCALE`) spent 26 ms of a
  39 ms step putting its image and 13 ms on the fire. `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565, so Eruption's palette is swapped at `XAllocColor`.
  Interference changes every pixel each frame; telling it the window is half
  the size changes its look (its wave table is in window pixels), so it stays
  at 10.2 fps.
- Kumppa rotates its picture with `XCopyArea` from the window onto itself.
  The fine checkerboard in its trails is the hack's: copies are checked
  against a read-everything-first reference in every overlap direction.
- Piecewise (`piecewise_direct.c`) is single precision with `single_frand.h`
  (67 to 42 ms) and frees each circle's high fringe, which upstream's free
  forgets (32 blocks a stop; `leaks` named `fringe_add_intersection`).
- BinaryRing (`binaryring_single.c`) is told the display is 24 bits deep: its
  16-bit path drops every hit below one 5-bit step, so only green builds up
  and the picture stays dim. Its pixels go straight to the window as it plots
  them, and the frame's `XPutImage` into a pixmap and copy back are skipped:
  the 32-bit image was put a pixel at a time, 130 of a 240 ms step.
  `tools/binaryring_patch.py` makes `frand1`'s exponent literal a float.
- GraphStat's word list (`graphstat.h`) is written from `vendor/` at build
  time (`firmware/graphstat_strings.py`). Its timing is in frames tuned for
  30 fps, so at 10 fps a picture takes about 36 s instead of 12.
- EtruscanVenus (`etruscanvenus_single_gl.c`) runs on a 48 by 32 grid
  (`tools/etruscanvenus_patch.py`, upstream's 192 by 128) at half resolution;
  `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMU`, `-DETRUSCANVENUS_NUMV` and `-DETRUSCANVENUS_FULL`
  try others. Its modes differ: those that fill the screen are fill-bound.
  `curlicue.h` is copied from `vendor/` at build time (`vendor_data.py`).
- BlockTube was dropped after Rod saw it (too slow, and not much going on);
  its source, notices row, `blocktube_single_gl.c`, `gl_textures.py` and
  `blocktube_patch.py` stay, the wrapper out of the build filter. To bring
  it back, add `pre:gl_textures.py` to the three `extra_scripts` and
  `blocktube` (with its `count_the_blocks`) to `patch_float_literals.py`
  again. It drew 400 blocks
  (`tools/blocktube_patch.py`, upstream's 1,000) at half resolution with a
  10 ms delay (`"*delay: 10000"` in its registry entry, now gone);
  fog is applied per block from the modelview's z when the hack
  sets the block's colour, and a block the fog hides is not drawn. There is
  no sphere map, so each face shows the whole texture. Its texture is
  converted from `vendor/` at build time (`gl_textures.py`). It also filters
  `glEnable` of fog and texture generation, which TinyGL warns about every
  frame.
- Companion Cube and Floppy are not ported (Rod dropped both, listed in
  `failed_ports.txt`). Each Companion Cube face draws a 9,588-vertex disc:
  about 71,000 vertices a cube, three cubes by default. Floppy's model is
  26,340 vertices (about 630 KB of floats, which would not fit beside the
  current firmware in the 3 MB app partition).
- Rocks and DecayScreen were wired, looked at and dropped in the 2026-10-12
  second batch, then brought back after Rod asked for the shim to be extended.
  Rocks stamps every rock bigger than 3 pixels with `XCopyPlane` from a
  depth-1 pixmap it filled with `XFillPolygon`, and the shim drew nothing into
  a bitmap, so only the far dots showed (a 3,000-frame dump looked nearly
  black): `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` now fill bitmaps. On the board it
  runs at 17.2 fps against its own 50 ms delay, and holds 2.66 MB of PSRAM and
  all but 32 KB of the internal heap while it runs (about 180 of its 400
  bitmaps are under the 4 KB internal limit); a rotation soak that left it for
  DecayScreen read heap and PSRAM back at their idle values. DecayScreen smears
  the picture `load_image_async_simple` paints (see `x11shim.md`); without one
  it stays black. Both were host-only findings from a frame dump: look at later
  frames (3,000) as well as 400 before pinning, and read what the hack draws
  with.
- Penrose (`penrose_short_pause.c`, `tools/penrose_patch.py`) restarts after
  900 frames (about 10 s at 87 fps) instead of 3,141 once the screen is full
  and 31,415 after an error it thinks it can recover from, about six minutes
  at the board's rate with nothing moving. Upstream counts those pauses in
  frames, tuned for a fast X server, so other devices show the same stall.
- Triangle's palette is `make_smooth_colormap`, which the shim now builds the
  way upstream picks it (two to five random colours, any saturation, never
  black): its first version was always a bright rainbow, and every hack that
  asks for a smooth map changed colour with the fix (24 pinned hashes moved,
  all looked at).
- Abstractile holds about 6.1 MB of PSRAM while it runs (the free PSRAM read
  883 KB), so it leaves little for anything else: it stops and restarts clean
  in the leak test, but watch it in a rotation soak. Lisa takes 87 ms a step
  as copied (9.6 fps) and 52 ms in single precision (`lisa_single.c`, 14.3
  fps) with frames that look the same but hash differently. Worm's worms are
  one pixel wide and there are only a few on a 466 pixel screen: plain, for
  Rod to judge. XRaySwarm's host frames are white bugs and trails; whether

"""PlatformIO pre-build script: rasterises Special Elite (Apache 2.0,
firmware/assets/fonts) into generated/special_elite.h in the build directory.
main.cpp hands it to the shim (xshim_set_font), and the Xft stand-in draws
XJack's text from it. The sizes are the ones XJack's font resources can land
on after the shim picks the nearest. Needs uv, because Pillow is not in
PlatformIO's Python."""

import shutil
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

Import("env")  # noqa: F821

project = Path(env["PROJECT_DIR"])  # noqa: F821
generated = Path(env.subst("$BUILD_DIR")) / "generated"  # noqa: F821
header = generated / "special_elite.h"
font = project / "assets" / "fonts" / "SpecialElite-Regular.ttf"
SIZES = "12,16,20,24"

uv = shutil.which("uv")
if not uv:
    raise SystemExit("the Xft font needs uv on PATH to rasterise Special Elite")
generated.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
fresh = generated / "special_elite.h.new"
subprocess.run(
    [
        uv,
        "run",
        str(project.parent / "tools" / "make_font_atlas.py"),
        str(font),
        "--name",
        "special_elite",
        "--sizes",
        SIZES,
        "-o",
        str(fresh),
    ],
    check=True,
)
if not header.exists() or header.read_bytes() != fresh.read_bytes():
    fresh.replace(header)
else:
    fresh.unlink()
env.Append(CPPPATH=[str(generated)])  # noqa: F821

content.content:
# Display, canvas and runner gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- M5GFX reads a plain `uint32_t` colour as RGB888. `TFT_RED` and friends are
  RGB565 constants. The canvas holds pixels already byte-swapped into the
  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits
  needs it (the logo loader, `dump_main.c`, tests). A hue-sweeping palette
  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and
  without a crash. `substrate_single.c` swaps at `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground` so the hack sees ordinary RGB565; its golden-frame test
  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.
- The display only gets the rows a hack drew. Every canvas write must go
  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`
  (which record a span per row), or call `canvas_mark_dirty`, or the screen
  keeps the old pixels. The overlay text in `main.cpp` is the one deliberate
  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.
  `test_push_present` replays every hack into a shadow display to catch a
  missed mark. M5GFX keeps a framebuffer for this panel and `endWrite` flushes
  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,
  0.1 ms apart). `push_plan` groups rows with a cost model fitted to device
  probes; its calibration shapes must include scattered rows, since compact
  rectangles cannot tell the models apart. Hacks that redraw unchanged pixels
  (CloudLife, Pedal) dirty nearly every row and gain little.
- The panel is round, so only the canvas's disc is pushed (issue #77).
  `canvas_set_disc` (in `main.cpp`) records each row's visible span: centre
  (w/2, h/2), and a pixel counts if any part of it is inside the circle.
  `push_plan` clips every dirty span to it and drops rows left empty. A hack
  with `sync_to_refresh` (Unknown Pleasures) still pushes whole rows, because
  its TE offset was swept for that push (#68). `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` turns off the
  push clip only, for an A/B: GL hacks still clear and fill only the disc
  (`gl.md`). Call `canvas_set_disc` before any `glshim_open`, which keeps a
  pointer to the spans. On the board: CloudLife's full frame 28.0 to 24.8 ms
  (26.2 to 28.4 fps), HexTrail 30.6 to 27.3 ms, Pyro 1.60 to 1.43 ms.
- Do not split a push into more batches than `push_plan`'s greedy grouping
  makes. Each extra flush in one push cost about 0.85 ms on the board, not the
  model's 17 us: a full disc frame in 19 bands took 39.9 ms against 24.7 ms in
  the greedy grouping's three, and per-row `pushImage` calls in one batch cost
  no more than one whole-image call (28.0 against 27.8 ms). The last flush of a
  push seems to finish while the hack draws its next frame; earlier ones are
  waited for. The cost model was fitted to single-flush pushes and cannot see
  this, so a split it rates cheaper can be slower.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".
- `M5.update()` samples the buttons only when it runs and keeps no edge, so a
  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.
- The runner caps a hack's delay at 10 s, and the loop credits only the push
  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,
  because a hack's delay is its pause after drawing. Compare device numbers
  with a baseline from the same build, not with old rows: Pyro fell from 30 to
  23 fps with no change to Pyro.
- `runner_start` paints the canvas in the hack's `background` resource before
  `init`, as `screenhack.c` paints the window, or black if it has none.
  Substrate is white; every other hack asks for black or nothing.
- Overlay modes cycle on a tap: nothing, name badge, QR code, fps, battery. The
  badge, the QR code and the info line share the stamp/unstamp path, and
  `kPatchMaxH` (100) must cover the tallest glyph plus its outline. The
  battery is polled every 30 s (`M5.Power.getBatteryLevel()`; negative means a
  failed read, so the last good level stays). The QR code is encoded once at
  boot with M5GFX's `lgfx_qrcode` (`buildQr`, lowest version that holds
  `QR_URL`) into a 328 px white square, the biggest square inside the round
  screen. Each frame only copies it over the canvas and back (it reuses
  `infoPatch`, so that buffer is sized for the QR), and 328 rows are pushed
  every frame while it shows. The badge stamps 48 outline copies per frame and
  adds about 16 to 20 ms to `push=`. Read `wait=` as well as fps: a hack with
  delay slack (Galaxy) hides it, one running flat out (Squiral) does not.
- `lgfx_qrcode.h` (M5GFX's QR encoder, included at the top of `main.cpp`)
  defines `MODE_*`, `ECC_*` and `LOCK_VERSION`, which clash with other code, so
  `main.cpp` `#undef`s them straight after the include. Its init returns
  nonzero when the text is too long for a version; `buildQr` tries versions 1
  to 40 and, if none fits, leaves `qrPixels` null so the tap cycle skips QR.
- Overlay text (`main.cpp`) is stamped into the canvas, pushed, then the
  pixels under it are restored. Drawing on the display after `pushImage`
  flickered badly, because the next push erases it. The canvas must end each
  frame exactly as the hack left it.
- Tearing. The panel scans its memory 60 times a second and `pushImage` is not
  synchronised with it, so for a refresh the top of the screen shows one
  picture and the rest another. A thin line that moves a few pixels a frame can
  fall in the gap and vanish for a frame (Unknown Pleasures' flicker: a flat
  stretch of one line gone for about 17 ms). The panel's TE line is on GPIO 38

  display's order (`rgb565()` returns them that way), and the display runs
  with `setSwapBytes(false)`. A swap done by M5GFX on each push cost 10 ms of
  every frame (#23: pushes of 41-45 ms became 31 ms). `px_swap()` turns a
  canvas pixel into ordinary RGB565 and back: only code that reads colour bits

  stays a rainbow with its bytes swapped (red, green and blue rotate), so only
  pure black and white, or a colour you know (Maze's red flame, its green
  solving path), expose a wrong order on the device. Host frames cannot,
  since the swap happens in the push; compare them with `px_swap` applied.
- A hack that takes colour bits out of pixel values itself (Substrate's alpha
  blend, in `point2rgb`) breaks on swapped pixels without a compile error and

  fails if either is missing. Searching for `XGetPixel` finds none of this:
  dump every hack before and after a pixel-format change and `cmp` the frames.
  Pyro differs by a few hundred pixels, because it sorts projectiles by pixel
  value and so draws overlaps in another order.
- The display only gets the rows a hack drew. Every canvas write must go
  through `canvas_clear`, `canvas_point`, `hspan` or `canvas_paste_rect`
  (which record a span per row), or call `canvas_mark_dirty`, or the screen
  keeps the old pixels. The overlay text in `main.cpp` is the one deliberate
  bypass: it is written straight into `px`, marked by hand, and restored with
  `canvas_paste_rect`, which marks it again so the next push erases it.
  `test_push_present` replays every hack into a shadow display to catch a
  missed mark. M5GFX keeps a framebuffer for this panel and `endWrite` flushes
  one bounding box around everything written in a `startWrite` batch, so rows
  far apart must not share a batch (two corner pixels cost 11.7 ms together,
  0.1 ms apart). `push_plan` groups rows with a cost model fitted to device
  probes; its calibration shapes must include scattered rows, since compact
  rectangles cannot tell the models apart. Hacks that redraw unchanged pixels
  (CloudLife, Pedal) dirty nearly every row and gain little.
- The panel is round, so only the canvas's disc is pushed (issue #77).
  `canvas_set_disc` (in `main.cpp`) records each row's visible span: centre
  (w/2, h/2), and a pixel counts if any part of it is inside the circle.
  `push_plan` clips every dirty span to it and drops rows left empty. A hack
  with `sync_to_refresh` (Unknown Pleasures) still pushes whole rows, because
  its TE offset was swept for that push (#68). `-DPUSH_NO_DISC` turns off the
  push clip only, for an A/B: GL hacks still clear and fill only the disc
  (`gl.md`). Call `canvas_set_disc` before any `glshim_open`, which keeps a
  pointer to the spans. On the board: CloudLife's full frame 28.0 to 24.8 ms
  (26.2 to 28.4 fps), HexTrail 30.6 to 27.3 ms, Pyro 1.60 to 1.43 ms.

  makes. Each extra flush in one push cost about 0.85 ms on the board, not the
  model's 17 us: a full disc frame in 19 bands took 39.9 ms against 24.7 ms in
  the greedy grouping's three, and per-row `pushImage` calls in one batch cost
  no more than one whole-image call (28.0 against 27.8 ms). The last flush of a
  push seems to finish while the hack draws its next frame; earlier ones are
  waited for. The cost model was fitted to single-flush pushes and cannot see
  this, so a split it rates cheaper can be slower.
- Hacks run on the Arduino `loopTask`, now set to a 16 KB stack in `main.cpp`.
  A hack with big local arrays can still overflow it (Rorschach's 9.6 KB did
  at 8 KB): the device reboots on that hack's first frame, and host tests
  cannot see it. Check the serial log for "Stack canary".

  press during a long hack step vanishes. `main.cpp` runs a 5 ms polling task
  on core 0 into `button_latch`, which needs the pin to hold a level for 30 ms.
  Reading the pin level inside a GPIO interrupt did not work: the release
  bounced and was counted as a second press. Check `press_waited` in the log.

  (31 ms; it was 41-45 ms between the byte-order fix and #23) against it,

# GitHub Flavored Markdown Generation

**Version:** 1.2.1

Generate GFM that passes markdownlint validation with zero violations.

## Core Principles

### 1. Blank Lines Are Mandatory

- Before/after ALL lists (MD032)
- Before/after ALL headings except document start (MD022)
- Before/after ALL code blocks (MD031)
- Between ALL block-level elements

### 2. Consistency Required

- Use `-` for lists
- Use `#` for headings (ATX)
- Regular spaces only—never tabs/nbsp

### 3. Structure Matters

- Heading hierarchy: 1→2→3 (not 1→3)
- ONE H1 per document
- Files end with one newline
- Lines under 80 chars

### 4. Invisible Characters Matter

- Use ONLY regular spaces (U+0020)
- Never non-breaking spaces (U+00A0,  )
- Never tabs
- UTF-8 encoding

## Pre-Generation Checklist

- [ ] Where will lists/headings/code appear?
- [ ] Heading levels verified (1→2→3)?
- [ ] Using `-` for all lists?
- [ ] Code languages specified?
- [ ] Lines under 80 chars?
- [ ] Line breaks needed? (two trailing spaces)
- [ ] Using regular spaces only?
- [ ] URLs wrapped in `<>` or `[]`?
- [ ] Document starts with H1?
- [ ] Ordered lists use `1.` for all items?
- [ ] File ends with single newline?
- [ ] Tables use consistent spacing?

## Essential Rules

### Lists (MD032, MD004)

```markdown
Text before.

- Item one
- Item two

Text after.
```

### Headings (MD001, MD022)

```markdown
Text.

## Heading

Content.
```

### Code Blocks (MD031, MD040)

````markdown
Text.

```python
code()
```

Text.
````

**Nested Fences:** When showing markdown examples that contain code blocks,
use **one more backtick** than the deepest level:

- Three backticks (` ``` `): Regular code
- Four backticks (` ```` `): Markdown examples with code
- Five backticks (` ````` `): Nested markdown examples

`````markdown
````markdown
# Example

```bash
command
```

````
`````

### Line Length (MD013)

Break long lines at natural points. Use reference-style links for long URLs.

### URLs and Email (MD034)

Wrap bare URLs and emails:

```markdown
Wrong: https://example.com
Right: <https://example.com>
Right: [link](https://example.com)

Wrong: user@example.com
Right: <user@example.com>
```

### Document Structure (MD041)

Start with H1 (or front matter then H1):

```markdown
# Document Title

First paragraph.
```

### Ordered Lists (MD029)

Use `1.` for all items:

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

### File Endings (MD047)

End with single newline:

```text
Last content line.
[single newline]
[EOF]
```

### Table Column Style (MD060)

Use consistent spacing in tables. Three styles:

**Compact (recommended):** `| cell |` - single space around content

```markdown
| Header 1 | Header 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Data | More data |
```

**Aligned:** Pipes vertically aligned with padding

**Tight:** `|cell|` - no spaces

Pick ONE style per document. Compact is preferred.

### Character Encoding

**Detection:** View → Render Whitespace in VS Code

**Fix:** Find `\u00A0` → Replace with space

**Critical for AI:** Two trailing spaces = intentional line breaks. Do NOT
remove them.

## Critical Error Patterns

### 1. List Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD032 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text:
- Item
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD032 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text:

- Item

Text.
```

### 2. Heading Without Blank Lines

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD022 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
Text.
## Head
Text.
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD022 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
Text.

## Head

Text.
```

### 3. Code Without Blanks/Language

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD031 MD040 -->

**Wrong:**

````markdown
Text:
```
code
```
Text.
````

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD031 MD040 -->

**Right:**

````markdown
Text:

```python
code
```

Text.
````

### 4. Inconsistent Markers

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD004 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
- Item
* Item
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD004 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
- Item
- Item
```

### 5. Skipping Levels

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD001 -->

**Wrong:**

```markdown
# Title

### Sub (skipped H2)
```

<!-- markdownlint-enable MD001 -->

**Right:**

```markdown
# Title

## Section

### Sub
```

## Post-Generation Validation

1. Lists have blank lines before/after
2. Headings have blank lines before/after
3. Code has blank lines before/after
4. Heading progression: 1→2→3→4
5. All lists use `-`
6. All code has language
7. Lines under 80 chars
8. Document starts with H1
9. URLs wrapped properly
10. Ordered lists use `1.`
11. File ends with one newline
12. Two trailing spaces used intentionally
13. Only regular spaces (no nbsp/tabs)
14. Tables use consistent column spacing

## Mental Model

Markdown is **blocks with mandatory spacing:**

```text
[Text Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Heading Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[List Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Code Block]
↓ BLANK LINE ↓
[Text Block]
[EOF]
```

````markdown
text
````

```markdown
1. item
1. item

text
```

**Table:**

```markdown
| Header | Header |
| --- | --- |
| Cell | Cell |

text
```

**Programming:** `python` `javascript` `java` `c` `cpp` `go` `rust` `ruby`
`php` `swift` `kotlin` `typescript`

**Shell:** `bash` `sh` `powershell` `cmd` `zsh`

**Markup:** `html` `css` `xml` `json` `yaml` `toml` `markdown`

**Database:** `sql` `postgresql` `mysql`

**Other:** `text` `diff` `log`

## Validation

```bash
markdownlint filename.md
```

Goal: Zero errors/warnings.

See bundled references:

- `references/complete-rules.md` - Full rule catalog
- `references/edge-cases.md` - Platform quirks
- `references/examples.md` - Detailed examples

Most common: Missing blank lines around lists/headings/code.

**Two trailing spaces:** Intentional line breaks. Do NOT remove.

## Xft text

A hack that draws with Xft (`XftDrawStringUtf8`, `load_xft_font_retry`) needs
the stand-in in `x11shim/xft.h`. Its font is Special Elite, rasterised at build
time into pixel-coverage tables (`firmware/font_atlas.py`, which runs
`tools/make_font_atlas.py` on the TTF in `firmware/assets/fonts/`), and
`main.cpp` installs it with `xshim_set_font`. Only ASCII has glyphs: anything
else draws as `?`. The family in a font name is ignored and the baked size
nearest the number is used, so to change a hack's text size override its font
resource (XJack's `XJACK_FONT_PX`) and bake the size in `font_atlas.py`.

Our `screenhack.h` does not include `xft.h`, because that would change what
every hack sees. Build the hack through a wrapper that includes it first
(`hacks/xjack_xft.c`), and exclude the original from all three
`build_src_filter` lines. XJack's wrapper shows two things an Xft hack may
need from `screenhack.c`: the window background set from the `background`
resource (`XClearWindow` otherwise clears to black), and a reshape after
init. Tests that run the hack install `test_font.h`'s blocky font, so a
pinned hash does not follow FreeType; with no font installed the shim gives a
blank one, so a test that replays every hack does not abort.

---
name: port-hack
description: Use when adding one or several xscreensaver hacks to the StopWatch firmware, choosing which hack to port next, or when a ported hack crashes, reboots, runs slowly, leaks memory or shows wrong colours on the device.
---

# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Threads, GL, Xft, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

## 4. Verify on the host

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such.

## 6. Deliver

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| "It is rated S, so I need not read it" | Maze was rated L for Xlib gaps; the real blocker was a 20 MB `calloc`. |
| "It compiles, so it works" | Rorschach compiled and rebooted on its first frame. |
| "The colours look right" | Not from a host frame: every hack was byte swapped until Maze. |
| "My test passes, so it tests something" | A test through Pyro passed with the runner broken. Break the code on purpose. |
| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |

content.text:
XJack is ported and passes everything on the host, but I haven't flashed it, so I can't say how it looks on the panel. It's on branch `feature/xjack-xft-text` in the `.claude/worktrees/xjack` worktree, with four commits and no PR yet.

**Host checks**
- **Native tests:** 741 of 741 pass.
- **Python tool tests:** 547 pass, with one skipped.
- **Notices check and markdownlint:** clean.
- **Device build:** compiles. Flash use rose from 87.0% to 88.8%, about 57 KB for the font tables.
- **Frames:** I looked at host dumps in the real font, and they show cream paper with black typewriter text, typos and scrolling. They are not yet viewed on the device.

**What I built**
- **Xft stand-in:** new `xft.c`, `xft.h` and `xft_font.h` in the shim. It blends glyphs onto the canvas and clips them, and is mutation-checked.
- **Font:** Special Elite (Apache 2.0, committed with its licence and a notices section). `tools/make_font_atlas.py` bakes it at 12, 16, 20 and 24 px at build time.
- **Wrapper:** `hacks/xjack_xft.c` includes `xjack.c` unmodified. I left `xft.h` out of `screenhack.h` because that would change what every hack sees.
- **Test font:** the tests use a blocky font, so the pinned hash doesn't follow FreeType. With no font installed the shim returns a blank one, because `test_pyro` and `test_push_present` replay every hack and XJack aborts without a font.

I didn't dig into graphstat's text code. It uses `texfont`, which draws GL quads, so it doesn't apply here.

**Two upstream quirks the wrapper works around**
- **Black page:** XJack clears the window, and the shim clears to black where `screenhack.c` uses the background colour. That gave black type on a black page.
- **Half-drawn lines:** `xjack_init` sizes the page before it sets its margins, and xscreensaver sends a reshape afterwards. Without it, lines were typed off the bottom and scrolled in half drawn.

Each fix has its own test, and the tests fail when the fix is removed.

**Decisions for you**
1. **Font size:** it's set to 16 px, from `-DXJACK_FONT_PX`. Upstream's 12 is small on this panel, and 20 reads well but gives about 28 columns. I can flash each pinned so you can pick.
2. **Shared shim fix:** the runner sends no reshape and doesn't default the window background. Fixing that in the runner would change every hack, so I didn't. Other light-background hacks that call `XClearWindow` may have the same fault. Do you want me to look?
3. **Flash and PR:** I'll flash only on your go-ahead, and I'll open a draft PR whenever you say.

**Not covered**
- Speed, memory use and the real colours on the panel are all unmeasured until it's flashed.
- The assessment's measured-rows file has no XJack row yet.

I haven't touched `AGENTS.md`; the new notes are in `.claude/rules/` and the port-hack skill.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/worktrees/xjack/.claude/skills/deliver-branch

# Delivering a branch

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md.

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  (`--type` takes only `bug`, `feature` or `task`; `chore` is refused)
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `gh pr merge N --merge` once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). His approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire
  Gates check to finish. A stacked PR's gate
  can fail "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges: if approvals
  and findings pass and the PR is mergeable, merge it, with no rebase.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.
- `entire agent-help` says trails are unavailable; `entire trail create` works.
  Write a PR body to a file for `gh pr edit --body-file` (an apostrophe in an
  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).
- `gh pr edit N --body-file` replaces the whole body, including the
  `<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->` ... `-end -->` block at the top. Keep that
  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.
- To file your own review's findings: `entire trail finding add --trail N
  --client-id <key> --severity high|medium|low --file <path> --start-line A
  --end-line B -m "<body>"` (no title flag; the client id makes a re-run safe).
  Open the body by saying an agent filed it for Rod.
- In a worktree session create the trail with a one-line `--body`, then set the
  real body with `gh pr edit N --body-file` (keep the trail-link block), and
  check `closingIssuesReferences` with `gh pr view N --json` (it can lag a
  few seconds).
- `entire trail update --body` takes no number and acts on the current
  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).
- Stacked PR: `entire trail create --base <parent-branch>`. When the parent
  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.
- `docs/porting-assessment.md` conflicts on rebase: `git checkout --theirs`
  it to continue, then rerun `tools/score_hacks.py` and amend the result in.
- Two ports in flight both append to `g_hacks[]`, so whichever merges second
  conflicts in `registry.c`, the expected list in `test_hacks.c`,
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, `tools/assessment_measured.md.in` (rows,
  paragraphs and the hack count) and the three `build_src_filter` lines in `platformio.ini`,
  as well as the generated assessment. Keep both sides, put the newer hack
  last, and regenerate the assessment. A rebased published branch needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod), and GitHub can reject that push once too.
- A finding that says the code "does not exist" can be stale after a rebase
  (the skill PR was reviewed before the Blaster and Substrate code it referred
  to had landed). Check it against `main` before dismissing, and put the
  evidence in the dismissal. Entire's approvals gate once showed "no reviewers
  have approved" right after a force push, though Rod had approved; his word is
  enough, so say so and go ahead.
- `entire trail finding list` can show one open "Review verdict ... approve"
  finding: it is the reviewers' verdict, not a defect. `mergeStateStatus`
  reads UNSTABLE while the gate runs, and Rod's approval is enough.
- A shared-code PR (stroker, runner, canvas) can move pins of hacks merged
  since it branched: merge or rebase onto `main` and rerun the pin loop before
  judging frames (Celtic joined #89's moved set after #88 landed).

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/trails/54
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Ports XJack, and adds an Xft text stand-in to the shim so it can draw. Written
by Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction.

## What changed

- **XJack** is copied unmodified (checked with `cmp`) and built through
  `hacks/xjack_xft.c`, which includes the stand-in first. It is last in
  `g_hacks[]` before the After Dark toasters.
- **Xft stand-in** (`x11shim/xft.c`, `xft.h`, `xft_font.h`; ours, MIT). It
  loads a font by the nearest baked size, measures text, and draws
  pre-rasterised ASCII glyphs alpha-blended onto the canvas, clipped in 64 bits
  and marked dirty. Anything outside ASCII draws as `?`. With no font installed
  a hack gets a blank one, because XJack `abort()`s without a font and
  `test_pyro` and `test_push_present` replay every hack.
- **Special Elite** (Apache 2.0, from google/fonts) is committed unchanged with
  its licence in `firmware/assets/fonts/`, and has a section in
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`. `tools/make_font_atlas.py` rasterises it at 12, 16,
  20 and 24 px at build time (`firmware/font_atlas.py`); `main.cpp` installs it.
  XJack defaults to 20 px (`-DXJACK_FONT_PX`): upstream's 12 was too small.
- **Wrapper fixes**, each with a test that fails without it. XJack clears the
  window, and the shim clears to black where `screenhack.c` uses the
  `background` resource, which gave black type on a black page. And
  `xjack_init` sizes the page before its margins, which xscreensaver corrects
  with a reshape after init: without one, lines typed at the bottom were
  clipped and scrolled up half drawn.
- Docs: the port-hack skill no longer lists Xft as unportable, and the shim and
  hack notes in `.claude/rules/` cover the stand-in and XJack.

## Verified

- **Compiles:** `pio run -e stopwatch` builds; flash is 88.8% of the app
  partition (87.0% before; the font tables are about 57 KB).
- **Host tests pass:** 741 of 741 native cases, 547 pytest (one skipped),
  `check_notices.py`, markdownlint, pre-commit. New tests are mutation-checked:
  20 of 22 mutants of `xft.c` die, and the two survivors only overflow
  off-canvas; 5 of 5 of the blank-font fallback; 8 of 8 of the font tool; and
  both wrapper fixes.
- **Runs on the device:** flashed pinned to XJack at 16 and then 20 px. Rod
  looked at it and said 20 looks good (colour, scrolling and layout).

## Not verified

- fps, step time and free heap and PSRAM on the board are unmeasured, and there
  is no row in `tools/assessment_measured.md.in` yet.
- No rotation soak with XJack in the registry.
- The pinned frame hash uses a blocky test font (`test_font.h`), so it does not
  follow FreeType; the real font is only seen on the panel.

## For Rod

- The runner sends no reshape and does not default the window background, which
  `screenhack.c` does. I fixed both in XJack's wrapper because changing the
  runner changes what every hack sees. Other light-background hacks that call
  `XClearWindow` may have the same fault: worth a look?
- `screenhack.h` does not include `xft.h`, for the same reason. The other Xft
  rows in the assessment (apollonian, fluidballs, memscroller, penetrate,
  noseguy) should now need only a wrapper like this one.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

#!/bin/bash
# Prints one line whenever something about PR 100 / trail 54 changes.
cd /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/worktrees/xjack || exit 1
prev=""
while true; do
  pr=$(gh pr view 100 --json state,isDraft,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision,headRefOid,comments,reviews --jq '"state=\(.state) draft=\(.isDraft) merge=\(.mergeStateStatus) review=\(.reviewDecision) head=\(.headRefOid[0:7]) comments=\(.comments|length) reviews=\(.reviews|length)"' 2>&1 || true)
  gates=$(gh api repos/rodbegbie/stopwatch-screensaver/commits/feature/xjack-xft-text/check-runs --jq '.check_runs[]|select(.name=="Entire Gates")|"\(.conclusion // .status): \(.output.summary|gsub("\n";" | "))"' 2>&1 || true)
  findings=$(entire trail finding list 54 </dev/null 2>&1 | head -8 | tr '\n' ' ' || true)
  cur="PR100: $pr
GATES: $gates
FINDINGS: $findings"
  if [ "$cur" != "$prev" ]; then
    echo "$cur"
    prev="$cur"
  fi
  case "$pr" in
    *state=MERGED*|*state=CLOSED*) exit 0 ;;
  esac
  sleep 60
done

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

# Adding a hack

Moved verbatim from AGENTS.md. The order of work is in `SKILL.md`.

The `port-hack` skill orders this work, says what to read for before copying a
hack, and holds a recipe per trap. The steps:

1. Check its row in `docs/porting-assessment.md` (effort and Speed band) and
   read its licence header.
2. Update the expected list in `firmware/test/test_hacks/test_hacks.c` and see
   it fail.
3. Copy the file to `firmware/src/hacks/<name>/<name>.c`, add the notices row
   and an `extern` plus entry in `hacks/registry.c`.
4. Fill shim gaps test-first in `firmware/test/test_xshim/`. The compile
   check in `score_hacks.py` shows what is missing.
5. Host tests pass, dump a frame and look at it, then (with Rod's go-ahead)
   flash and measure fps and free heap/PSRAM over serial. To pin its frame
   hash after looking at the frame, put `0x1ull` in `kBaseline`, run
   `pio test -e native -f test_hacks`, convert the "Was N" in the failure line
   with `python3 -c "print(hex(N))"`, and run it again.
6. Regenerate the assessment and add measurements to
   `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, then re-run the speed backtest: each port
   adds a point to the check of the Speed bands, which were fitted to the first
   29 hacks. To make a port a real test, commit its host time and predicted
   range first (`docs/speed-predictions.md` shows the form), flash it as copied,
   and add its name to `HOLDOUT` in `tools/speed_backtest.py`. The first four
   (Mountain, Epicycle, Kaleidescope, Celtic) all fell where predicted.
7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (for a
   plain screenhack, `hacks/substrate_single.c`; the recipe is in the skill's
   `techniques.md`), and compare double and float frames at several frame
   counts. A resource
   override can skip a hack's restart cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so
   leak-test any override.
8. If Rod drops a port after seeing it (Hypnowheel, Boing; Celtic was dropped
   and came back through issue #37): remove it
   from `g_hacks[]`, the expected list, its hash and its leak test; keep the
   source and notices row; add `name: reason` (short: it is printed as a
   bullet) to `tools/failed_ports.txt`. For a GL hack, keep the `<name>_gl.c`
   wrapper but exclude it and the directory (`-<hacks/boing/>
   -<hacks/boing_gl.c>`) in all three `build_src_filter` lines, or it still
   builds. A reason Rod gave in his own words ("boring on a small screen") is
   the reason to record. File an issue only if there is something to come back

  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body, then read the PR back (`gh pr view N --json body`):
  #27 merged with the generic body, so `Fixes #23` never reached GitHub and
  the issue stayed open until it was closed by hand.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`. Confirm the merge
  after a fresh `git fetch`: a stale `origin/main` says "not merged". Remove
  the branch's worktree first (a checked-out branch cannot be deleted), and
  note that `git branch -d` refuses while local `main` is behind, so check
  `git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main` and then use `-D`. `main` is
  usually checked out in Rod's main checkout, so `git fetch origin main:main`
  is refused there: run `git merge --ff-only origin/main` in it, only if
  `git status` shows no tracked changes.
- Merge with `gh pr ready N` then `gh pr merge N --merge` once Rod approves
  (trail PRs are drafts). His approval is enough: do not wait for the Entire
  Gates check to finish. A stacked PR's gate
  can fail "Up to date: 1 commit behind" once its parent merges: if approvals
  and findings pass and the PR is mergeable, merge it, with no rebase.
- Before merging, `git fetch` and compare the PR's `headRefOid` with your tip:
  Rod sometimes pushes to the branch (docs commits, a merge of `main`). Read
  what arrived with `git log --oneline <tip>..origin/<branch>`, and clean up
  from the merge commit, not your last push. After `ExitWorktree keep` the
  tool names the branch `worktree-<name>`; the real branch is
  `git worktree list`'s.
- A review of fixed code can raise a new finding on the fix itself (a clamp
  that did not stop a wrap). Reproduce it with a failing test before changing
  the code, and mutation-check each branch of the new guard.

  inline `--body '...'` must be `'"'"'`).

  block in the file, or the PR loses its trail.

  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes. `N` is the trail number (PR #12 was
  trail 6), not the PR number. For a false positive or upstream behaviour in a
  byte-identical hack, use `entire trail finding dismiss N <id> -m "<reason>"`.

  branch (`entire trail update 8` errors).

  merges, `gh pr edit N --base main` before deleting its branch, then
  `git rebase --onto origin/main <old parent tip>`. The rebased push needs
  `--force-with-lease` (ask Rod first), unless the branch was never pushed.

"""Reads the StopWatch's serial log into a file for a number of seconds.

    .venv/bin/python -I tools/serial_capture.py <out-file> <seconds> [port]

Opening the port resets the board (a random hack starts, the overlay returns to
nothing), and a flash or a crash makes the port go away and come back, so this
reopens it in a loop. Run it in the background with absolute paths; background
shells ignore `cd`. The `run <hack> fps= step= push= ...` lines are explained in
AGENTS.md ("Serial log").
"""

import sys
import time

import serial

DEFAULT_PORT = "/dev/cu.usbmodem112401"


def capture(out: str, seconds: float, port: str = DEFAULT_PORT) -> None:
    end = time.time() + seconds
    with open(out, "wb") as f:
        while time.time() < end:
            try:
                with serial.Serial(port, 115200, timeout=1) as s:
                    while time.time() < end:
                        f.write(s.read(4096))
                        f.flush()
            except (serial.SerialException, OSError):
                time.sleep(0.5)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) not in (3, 4):
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    capture(sys.argv[1], float(sys.argv[2]), *(sys.argv[3:]))
#!/bin/bash
# Flashes a build that starts on one hack with rotation off, then reads the
# serial log. Needs the board, and Rod's say-so in the session (AGENTS.md:
# never flash without asking, unless he has said it is allowed).
#
#   bash tools/flash_and_capture.sh <hack> <seconds> [extra build flags] [lines]
#
# <hack> is a name from g_hacks[] in any case; extra flags are things like
# "-DFIREWORKX_SCALE=2"; the last `run` lines (default 6) are printed. The full
# log and the flash output go to $OUT_DIR (default: ./flash-capture, which
# should be somewhere git ignores, such as your scratchpad).
set -u
[ $# -ge 2 ] || { sed -n '2,12p' "$0"; exit 2; }
hack=$1 seconds=$2 extra=${3:-} lines=${4:-6}
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
out=${OUT_DIR:-./flash-capture}
mkdir -p "$out"
out=$(cd "$out" && pwd)

source "$repo/tools/env.sh"
cd "$repo/firmware" || exit 1
PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS="-DSTART_HACK=\\\"$hack\\\" -DROTATE_SECONDS=0 $extra" \
  NO_COLOR=1 pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > "$out/flash_$hack.txt" 2>&1
pio_status=$?
unset PLATFORMIO_BUILD_FLAGS
verified=$(grep -c 'Hash of data verified' "$out/flash_$hack.txt")
echo "flash verified: $verified" "$(grep -E 'Flash:' "$out/flash_$hack.txt")"
grep -E "error:|overflowed" "$out/flash_$hack.txt" | head -3
# A failed flash leaves the old firmware running, and the capture would measure
# that: stop rather than report numbers for the wrong build.

content.content:
## Measured on the device

Eighty hacks have been run so far (default settings, 466×466 canvas
pushed to the display every frame, canvas held in PSRAM). The firmware times
each frame in three parts, averaged over 5 seconds: **step** is the hack's own
draw call, **push** is sending the canvas to the display, and **wait** is what
is left of the delay the hack asked for once the push is credited against it
(the runner caps any delay at 10 seconds). Rows other than Rorschach and Pedal
were measured before the cap was raised from 1 second; Helix also asks for
5-second holds, so its frame rate will now be lower than shown.

| Hack | fps | step | push | wait | Extra PSRAM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pyro | 30.0 | 0.8-1.1 ms | 31.2 ms | 0 ms | about 80 KB |
| Lisa (as copied) | 9.6 | 87.5 ms | 12.6-13.3 ms | 5.7 ms | none measurable |
| Lisa | 14.2-14.4 | 51.9-52.5 ms | 12.7-14.2 ms | 4.2-5.7 ms | none measurable |
| Penrose | 77.4-89.6 | 0.0-0.9 ms | 0.1-1.0 ms | 10.9-11.7 ms | none measurable |
| Worm | 51.6 | 0.3 ms | 1.3-1.4 ms | 17.7 ms | about 164 KB |
| Triangle | 57.4-67.0 | 3.6-6.0 ms | 0.9-2.1 ms | 9.3-10.4 ms | about 145 KB |
| XRaySwarm | 22.8-23.0 | 21.2-21.6 ms | 0.9-2.8 ms | 19.4-21.6 ms | about 59 KB |
| Rocks | 17.2-17.4 | 2.5-3.2 ms | 3.5-4.7 ms | 50.7-52.0 ms | about 2.66 MB |
| DecayScreen | 63.6-66.8 | 3.3-3.9 ms | 4.3-5.0 ms | 6.7-7.3 ms | none measurable |

The rows from Abstractile to XRaySwarm are the batch of 2026-10-12 (Abstractile,
Attraction, Greynetic, Wander, PopSquares, Lisa, Penrose, Worm, Triangle and
XRaySwarm), each from a pinned build with rotation off, read for 45 s (the
first window dropped) with Rod's go-ahead to flash. "Extra PSRAM" is the drop
from 6,989,667 bytes; good to about 10 KB. Abstractile holds about 6.1 MB
while it runs, leaving under 1 MB of PSRAM. Lisa is registered in single
precision (`lisa_single.c`): 9.6 fps as copied, 14.3 after. Rocks and
DecayScreen were added in a second pass, once the shim filled bitmaps and
painted a picture for a screen grab; Rocks holds 2.66 MB of PSRAM and leaves

# Scorer and speed-prediction gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- `score_hacks.py` rates effort by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps, and Braid was rated S and
  runs at 3-9 fps. The Speed column runs the hack on the host instead and ranks
  the device step well (Spearman about 0.9 over the 29 hacks it was fitted to,
  and four more ported since fell where predicted), but a low band does not
  clear a hack that does software `double` maths: the device ran 60-1,500
  times the host time, most for the double-bound ones. It says nothing about
  memory: Celtic as copied held about 300 KB of the 325 KB of free heap and
  ran at 1.2 fps (it is registered again after issue #37, see `hacks.md`). A
  failed port that has its source and a measured row (Hypnowheel, Boing)
  still counts in `speed_backtest.py`, probed standalone. Measure on the
  device, and read
  `docs/speed-backtest.md` before trusting a band. A hack with gaps (M and
  above) cannot be built, so it has no Speed.
- A `failed_ports.txt` name is the scorer's: the source file's stem
  (`companion` for Companion Cube), as the assessment's rows spell it. Check
  the cross appears after regenerating.
- `score_hacks.py --no-probe` also blanks the Speed column of the generated
  assessment ("high (2 ms)" becomes "-"): commit the output of a full run. The
  backtest reads a measured row only when its name is the bare hack name
  (`| Deluxe |`); a row with a note in brackets is skipped, so put the build
  that is registered in the bare row.
- `score_hacks.py` counts a hack as ported if `&<name>_hack` appears anywhere

metadata:

XJack and the Xft stand-in merged as PR #100 (trail 54, merge 530cb8f, 2026-10-12). Branch and worktree are deleted and `main` is fast-forwarded. Special Elite (Apache 2.0, google/fonts) is baked at 12/16/20/24 px by `tools/make_font_atlas.py`; XJack defaults to 20 px (`-DXJACK_FONT_PX`), which Rod picked on the panel after finding 12 and 16 small.

Measured the same day from the pinned build, 350 s: 7.8-15.8 fps, paced by its own delay (`wait` 46-130 ms); typing is a 0.1 ms step, scrolling 3.9-13.8 ms with 74-241 row pushes; no PSRAM held; internal heap fell 352 B in three steps (303,600 to 303,248), not known whether a leak. Row and paragraph are on branch `chore/xjack-measurements` (8c15639), unpushed until Rod says.

**Why:** the skill used to call Xft hacks unportable; other Xft rows (apollonian, fluidballs, memscroller, penetrate, noseguy) now only need a wrapper like `hacks/xjack_xft.c`.

**How to apply:**
- The board still holds a build pinned to XJack at 20 px with rotation off. It needs a plain rebuild and flash to rotate again; ask Rod first ([[feedback-flash-only-with-explicit-approval]]).
- No rotation soak with XJack yet; `docs/speed-backtest.md` not regenerated (a hack with two phases gives the backtest no single number).
- A measured row's fps cell must be a plain numeric range or `probe_hacks.parse_measured` skips it and the assessment shows `-`.
- Open question put to Rod: the runner sends no reshape and `XClearWindow` clears to black, unlike `screenhack.c`. Fixed only in XJack's wrapper because changing the runner changes every hack; other light-background hacks may have the fault. `screenhack.h` deliberately does not include `xft.h` for the same reason.
- Tests use `test_hacks/test_font.h`'s blocky font so pins do not follow FreeType; with no font the shim gives a blank one (test_pyro and test_push_present run every hack and XJack abort()s on none).

content.text:
I've measured XJack on the board from a 350-second capture of the pinned 20 px build. XJack is paced by its own delay, so its frame rate says little about the board. The write-up is committed on `chore/xjack-measurements` (`8c15639`) and is not pushed. That branch is checked out in your main checkout.

**What the board showed**
- **Frame rate:** 7.8–15.8 fps, with `wait` of 46–130 ms.
- **Typing, the first 25 s:** 7.8–9.2 fps, a 0.1 ms step, and a 0.3 ms push of 10 rows a frame.
- **Scrolling, once the page is full:** 8.8–15.8 fps (mean 11.6), a 3.9–13.8 ms step, and pushes of 74–241 rows (mean 150), taking 4.3–15.0 ms.
- **Host comparison:** the host step is 0.003 ms, so the board ran roughly 30 times the host while typing.
- **Memory:** no PSRAM held, and PSRAM didn't move (6,989,667 B throughout).
- **Internal heap:** it fell 352 B in three steps, from 303,600 B at boot to 303,248 B, and was flat otherwise. A 6-minute run can't say whether that is a leak.
- **Faults:** no stack canary, panic or reboot. The one reset in the log is from opening the port.

**What I committed:** the measured row and a paragraph in `tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, a regenerated `docs/porting-assessment.md`, and the "unmeasured" line in `hacks.md`. The assessment's XJack row now reads "0.1-13.8 ms measured". The other speed figures in the regenerated assessment shifted a little from host-timing jitter. The tool tests pass (547, one skipped).

**Still open**
- Whether to push this as a PR or straight to `main`. Your note says `AGENTS.md` goes straight to `main`, but measured rows have gone through PRs before, so I haven't pushed.
- I haven't regenerated `docs/speed-backtest.md`, because a two-phase hack gives the backtest no single number.
- There's been no rotation soak with XJack in the registry.
- The board is still on the pinned XJack build, and getting it back into rotation needs a plain reflash on your go-ahead.
